messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] How does rqtl behave when the allele distribution at one locus is widely different from the expected one?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] How does rqtl behave when the allele distribution at one locus is widely different from the expected one?
messages.body_plain:
A similar issue would arise in analysis of variance more generally, when one group has a much smaller sample size than the others. But the image you should looks to me like a real effect.

My main concern would be that the null distribution of the LOD score would be different for this chromosome than for others. So I'd be inclined to use a separate significance threshold for this chromosome than for others.

karl

> On Mar 30, 2015, at 2:50 AM, aspergi...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I am analysing an intercross of mice characterized by different susceptibility to induced lung tumorigenesis depending on the genotype at a single major locus. In detail, mice that are "aa" at this locus generally don't develop lung tumors after treatment with a chemical mutagen, while "AA" and "Aa" mice develop from 3-4 to 30 lung tumors per individual.
>
> In this intercross, we are carrying out an eQTL study in lung tumor tissue to find out if the expression levels of specific genes are under quantitative control of the tumor-susceptibility locus. However, since "aa" mice develop lung tumors only in rare cases, we only characterized 8 "aa" lung tumor tissue samples versus around 60 "AA" (each from a different mouse) and 60 "Aa". This means that - only at this locus - our population does not respect the expected genotype frequency.
>
> My question is: Rqtl finds many more statistically significant eQTLs (around 800 target genes) at this locus than for any other locus in the genome (the median of targets per locus is around 5-10). While this can have a biological meaning (the different tumor susceptibility of our cross is mediated by this locus and we are examining gene expression in tumor tissue), I have some doubts that rqtl is somehow getting "confused" by the wrong genotype distribution. Indeed, when I examine the expression levels of the target genes of this locus, I often observe that there is no difference at all between the distribution of the expression levels in AA and Aa mice, while aa mice have only slightly different expression levels, with a very wide distribution (probably due to the very small number of sampled individuals). For instance, in the attached example, rqtl finds a QTL with LOD 9 at this locus (significance threshold with 10,000 perms = 4.5), but I think that the variation of the expression levels is questionable.
>
> Does anyone have any idea on this?
>
> Thank you very much!
>
>
> Chiara
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

As a relative new user of R-qtl, I found this page very useful. With respect to my own research, I have some trouble in trusting the obtained data.
I'm trying to detect QTLs for a type of abiotic stress tolerance in tomato.
Because phenotyping is a major bottleneck in this research, I have only 96 individuals and 126 markers, which might become though to do QTL on.

So far, I've performed scanone, stepwise and mqmscan analysis on the data.
>From the  scanone output I did find some insignificant "peaks",  (1000 permutations)
Using the stepwise function, I do find a model with interacting QTLs (1000 permutations), corresponding to the peaks obtained in the scanone function (see script below). Remarkable, is that I only find a model when I increase the max number of QTLs. If this is lower then 12, no model is detected.
Using mqmscan, the peaks found in scanone do overlap and become significant (1000 permutations), but using mqmgetmodel, I do not get a model.

Therefore, I am confused and highly doubt my output. Am I overlooking something or is such output trustworthy?

Any comment is much appreciated,

Kind regards,

Nicky

STEPWISE
simv7<-sim.geno(d5v7nmkos)
perms1000imp<-scantwo(simv7, method="imp", pheno.col=13, n.perm=1000)
penal1000<-calc.penalties(perms1000imp, alpha=0.05)

step7_15p<-stepwiseqtl(simv7, pheno.col=13, max.qtl=15, penalties=penal1000,
                       keeptrace=TRUE, keeplodprofile=TRUE)

messages.subject: Re: Model comparison scanone, stepwise and MQM differ
messages.subject_clean: Model comparison scanone, stepwise and MQM differ
messages.body_plain:
I have not encountered not obtaining a model from stepwiseqtl(), but here are a couple of things I would check:

(a) See if your (main, heavy, and light) penalties from your two-dimensional scan for stepwiseqtl() analyses are in or near the same range as the penalties for mouse intercross from Manichaikul et al. (2009)  (3.52, 4.28, 2.69). Your penalties won't be the same, but in my experience with plant phenotypes from a biparental cross (using 24k permutations), penalties hover near or two-fold larger than these values. Perhaps increasing scantwo() permutations or trying default penalties will yield a model with less than 12 QTL.

(b) Initialize the stepwiseqtl() with the QTL model from your scanone analysis. For example, if you saw a QTL on chromosome N at position A and another QTL on chromosome M at position B:
     init_qtl <- makeqtl(inputcross, chr=c(N,M), pos=c(A,B))
     stepout <- stepwiseqtl(inputcross, pheno.col=phenotype, qtl=init_qtl, formula=y~Q1+Q2, ....)

Finally, if you're looking for a model with few false-positives, I like to follow the Manichaikul et al (2009) procedure in selecting a model based on penalties after performing stepwiseqtl() and not just the model with largest pLOD.

Sandra Truong

messages.subject: Advanced intercross and backcross design
messages.body_plain:
Greetings,

I'm wondering if it is possible to analyze a specific type of cross on R/QTL. I realize the BCsFt tools allow for analysis of [a series of] backcrosses followed by [a series of] intercrossing. My question is: can one analyze a cross created by first a intercrossing for multiple generations and THEN backcrossing (say, once or twice)? It's clear that the resultant mapping populations between these two approached necessarily differs, as the former will contain all possible genotype combinations at any given locus (A/A, A/a, a/a) but the latter can only contain two (A/A, A/a). I'm just not sure how the new advanced crosses feature of R/QTL deals with that.

Cheers,
Yasir

messages.subject: Re: integration of parental linkage maps?
messages.body_plain:
Hello guys

I think my question was a bit silly and for this remained unanswered.
However I found you can integrate the parental linkage maps.

- You make one map for each parent
- You insert the common markers
- You find the linkage group of the parent1 associated  with linkage groups of the parent2
- You combine the raw data
-  You re-calculate the map

Best,
Loukas

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] no qtl from scanone, need scantwo?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] no qtl from scanone, need scantwo?
messages.body_plain:
"need" is hard to answer.

If you've got 30,000 phenotypes and lots of interesting things to investigate, you might want to make the effort to investigate interactions in such traits to a low priority.

But if you've got two traits and see nothing in scanone, you probably want to do a bit more investigation, to try to find _something_ from the study.

It's true that you may find loci in scantwo when you saw nothing in scanone. The probability of this is not very high, but it can certainly happen.

karl
